question: When an analyst replaces part of a Transformer with a lower-dimensional, clustered, or hard-attention proxy that agrees with the original model on familiar inputs, does that proxy continue to predict the original model's behavior under systematic distribution shifts?

key_findings.claim: The experiments directly intervene on a trained model rather than merely comparing visualizations, which is the paper's strongest methodological contribution.
key_findings.evidence: For each attention head, the authors collect key and query embeddings from 1,000 training sequences, either project them onto the top k right-singular directions of their concatenation or replace them by separately fitted k-means centers, and then recompute attention and downstream predictions. A third intervention replaces soft attention by a one-hot distribution on the highest-scoring key.

key_findings.claim: On the controlled Dyck task, training-fitted low-rank and clustered proxies agree much better with the original model on previously seen bracket structures than on unseen structures or depths.
key_findings.evidence: The original two-layer, one-head-per-layer Transformer reaches nearly perfect structural generalization and about 75% depth generalization. The second-layer key/query representation can be reduced to about four SVD dimensions while retaining nearly 100% top-1 prediction agreement on Seen struct, yet agreement and attention-distribution similarity deteriorate on unseen structures and depth, across three training seeds.

anchors.section: Appendix A.2-A.3, model and training details

key_findings.claim: The Dyck comparison is not a clean IID-versus-OOD test because the headline 'Seen struct' control is a rare, short, selected conditioning event rather than a representative fresh sample from the training generator.
key_findings.evidence: Seen struct retains only bracket structures observed among 200,000 training strings and has maximum length 30. Appendix A.1 constructs a true held-out IID draw from the same generator, observes that almost all of it has unseen structures, and says its simplification results are nearly identical to Unseen structure (length greater than 32). Thus the proxy fails on typical IID draws as well; the main contrast is largely seen/easy structure versus novel/typical structure.

anchors.section: Section 2, Dyck structural splits and footnote 3

key_findings.claim: The abstract's statement that the proxies accurately approximate the full model 'on the training set' is not behaviorally demonstrated.
key_findings.evidence: The SVD and clustering fits use a sample of 1,000 training sequences, but the reported agreement baseline is the held-out Seen struct set. No train-set prediction-similarity curve, attention divergence, or train-versus-test reconstruction analysis is reported, so fitting on training activations should not be conflated with demonstrated behavioral fidelity on the training set.

anchors.section: Section 3, Simplifying key and query embeddings

key_findings.claim: The paper does not separate loss of a low-variance but causally important feature from ordinary deterioration of the approximation under representation shift.
key_findings.evidence: SVD and k-means are deliberately fitted only to training-distribution activations. The study reports output agreement and Jensen-Shannon divergence of attention, but not held-out explained variance, key/query reconstruction error, subspace angle, distance to cluster centers, or controls fitted on OOD activations. A larger OOD representation error is therefore a sufficient alternative explanation for some downstream fidelity gaps.

key_findings.claim: Top-1 Same Prediction is sensitive to the original model's logit margin, so a shift in confidence can create a fidelity gap even at matched internal approximation error.
key_findings.evidence: The binary indicator changes when any perturbation crosses the winning-logit boundary. OOD sequences can differ in length, attention entropy, activation norms, difficulty, and base-model margin; filtering CodeSearchNet to tokens the original predicts correctly does not match these variables. The paper includes no margin-stratified, equal-reconstruction-error, random-projection, or calibrated-noise control.

anchors.section: Appendix B.6, significance and correct/incorrect subsets

key_findings.claim: Hard attention can outperform the original model at unseen depths, but this demonstrates a changed inductive bias rather than a predictably conservative simplification.
key_findings.evidence: Replacing the second-layer soft distribution by one-hot attention is faithful on most Dyck splits yet slightly improves accuracy at deeper unseen nesting levels, including cases where the original attends most strongly to the correct location. The intervention removes secondary attended positions and changes the computed function; it is therefore a useful counterexample to assuming that simpler proxies merely underestimate the source model.

key_findings.claim: The CodeSearchNet experiment reproduces a language-shift gap, but the result is shift-specific rather than universal.
key_findings.evidence: Four-layer, four-head character models trained on 202,395 Java functions show lower SVD proxy agreement on JavaScript, Go, and PHP than on held-out Java. There is no discernible gap on deeper Java functions. Unseen languages also change syntax, token and context frequencies, average function length, base accuracy, and confidence, and the analysis does not construct matched subsets that isolate language identity from those factors.

anchors.section: Appendix B.6, Table 2 and significance test

key_findings.claim: The proposed link between 'algorithmic' subtasks and larger fidelity gaps is descriptive and substantially confounded.
key_findings.evidence: Repeated-word and close-bracket predictions exhibit relatively large gaps, while whitespace, separators, and other locally predictable characters exhibit smaller ones. These categories also differ in frequency, sequence position, logit margin, base-model error, relevant heads, and contextual redundancy. No interaction test, matched-difficulty comparison, or causal intervention establishes algorithmicity as the driver.

key_findings.claim: The claimed induction-head example is a plausible visual hypothesis, not a validated circuit interpretation.
key_findings.evidence: The fourth head in the fourth layer has the largest rank-16 gap for repeated-word predictions, and two displayed patterns look induction-like. The paper does not perform activation/path patching, causal scrubbing, feature interventions, or a held-out detector test to establish that this head and its compressed-away directions implement the proposed mechanism.

anchors.section: Appendix B.6, Which attention head is associated with the biggest gap?

key_findings.claim: The CodeSearchNet significance calculation has only three independent seed pairs and does not address repeated testing across simplification levels.
key_findings.evidence: For each rank, head scores are first averaged within each of three model initializations and a paired t-test compares Java with aggregated OOD scores, yielding p at most 0.005. With n=3 pairs the normality assumption is fragile, exact effect estimates and confidence intervals are not tabulated, and separate tests across ranks receive no multiplicity correction.

key_findings.claim: The SCAN appendix contains test-set model selection and pseudoreplicated uncertainty, so it is weak corroborating evidence.
key_findings.evidence: The authors search layer and head counts and select the architecture with highest accuracy on the Add-jump or length generalization split that is then analyzed. Figure 20 reports 95% intervals averaged over attention heads, although heads within a trained model are not independent experimental replicates. Add-jump shows no discernible gap and length shows only a small one.

key_findings.claim: The empirical scope is far narrower than the paper's safety-facing framing of mechanistic interpretation.
key_findings.evidence: Only keys and queries from one attention head at a time are altered; values, output projections, MLPs, residual streams, and whole circuits are not jointly simplified. The main models are a width-32 two-layer synthetic Transformer and a width-256 four-layer character model, with three seeds and no modern pretrained language model or deployment behavior.

key_findings.claim: Failure of an intervened proxy to reproduce a model under shift does not by itself falsify a mechanistic interpretation stated and tested on the original model.
key_findings.evidence: SVD or clustering can inspire a hypothesis about a feature, but a researcher can then test that hypothesis through interventions on the unmodified model. The experiments establish that compressed surrogate functions may be unfaithful outside their fitting distribution; they do not show that all human-readable circuit hypotheses derived with those visual aids are illusory. The broad conclusion should therefore be limited to proxy-based behavioral extrapolation unless the interpretation itself is operationalized and causally tested.

method.core_idea: Turn common representational simplifications into executable proxy models and compare their behavior with the original Transformer on familiar and systematically shifted inputs.
method.mechanism: Fit SVD subspaces or k-means codebooks to training-distribution key/query activations, replace the relevant activations at inference, recompute attention and the remaining network, and measure attention divergence plus top-1 prediction agreement. Compare these data-dependent proxies with a data-independent hard-attention intervention on Dyck, then repeat per head on Java-to-other-language CodeSearchNet and SCAN splits.
assumptions: High-variance or frequently occupied activation directions contain the features needed for the mechanism of interest.
Agreement on Seen struct is an informative in-distribution proxy-fidelity baseline.
A drop in top-1 agreement mainly reflects missing mechanistic features rather than changed logit margins or larger raw projection error.
Replacing only keys and queries leaves a proxy whose errors can be interpreted locally at that attention head.
Systematic shifts in bracket structure, depth, programming language, or SCAN composition are relevant tests of extrapolative interpretability.
Three training seeds adequately characterize variability across learned algorithms.
Character-prediction categories meaningfully distinguish algorithmic from local language-modeling computations.
A simplified executable model is representative of the mechanistic interpretation an analyst would draw from its visualization.

techniques.role: Fits a joint low-rank subspace to concatenated key and query embeddings from 1,000 training sequences.
Projects live key and query activations before recomputing attention and the model output.
Quantizes keys and queries into separately fitted cluster centers.
Replaces soft attention by mass on the highest-scoring key as a data-independent simplification.
Measures distributional discrepancy between original and simplified attention patterns.
Measures behavioral proxy fidelity by exact agreement with the original model's winning token.
Separates previously seen structures, unseen structures by length, and unseen nesting depth.
Applies SVD independently to each head of a character-level CodeSearchNet Transformer.
Breaks code results into repeated words, brackets, whitespace, separators, and other character classes.
Uses low-dimensional plots and example attention maps to propose depth and induction-like mechanisms.

evaluations.setting: Dyck-(20,10), 200,000 training strings and 20,000 strings per evaluation split; two-layer, one-head-per-layer Transformer with hidden size 32 and three seeds
evaluations.metric: Closing-bracket accuracy, attention Jensen-Shannon divergence, and Same Prediction versus SVD rank or cluster count
evaluations.result: Original models nearly perfectly generalize to unseen structures and reach about 75% on unseen depth; low-dimensional proxies are almost perfectly faithful on Seen struct but substantially less faithful on unseen structures and depths.
evaluations.baseline: No random projection/noise, matched reconstruction-error, OOD-fitted subspace, or representative IID behavioral baseline in the main figures.

evaluations.metric: Same Prediction and closing-bracket accuracy across structural and depth splits
evaluations.result: Hard attention is faithful on all but depth generalization and slightly outperforms the original model at high unseen depths.
evaluations.baseline: A function-changing intervention rather than a capacity-matched or error-matched proxy.

evaluations.setting: CodeSearchNet character modeling: four layers, four heads per layer, model size 256, head size 64, three seeds; train on 202,395 shallow Java functions and test Java, deeper Java, JavaScript, Go, and PHP
evaluations.metric: Original-model accuracy and SVD Same Prediction, primarily on tokens the original predicts correctly
evaluations.result: Proxy fidelity is lower on unseen programming languages than Java at every tested rank, while no discernible gap appears for deeper Java functions.
evaluations.baseline: No margin-matched, length-matched, syntax-matched, random-projection, or OOD-reconstruction controls.

evaluations.metric: Java-minus-unseen-language Same Prediction gap by character category and attention head
evaluations.result: Repeated-word and close-bracket categories have larger gaps; one late head appears induction-like and one early head appears locally bigram-oriented.
evaluations.baseline: Descriptive stratification and two visual examples, without a causal circuit or statistical interaction test.

evaluations.setting: SCAN Add-jump and length generalization with architectures selected for accuracy on the corresponding generalization split
evaluations.metric: Attention approximation quality after per-head SVD or clustering
evaluations.result: No discernible Add-jump gap and a small, consistent length gap are reported.
evaluations.baseline: Architecture selection uses the evaluation shift, and confidence intervals treat dependent heads as replicate units.

limitations: [Reviewer-identified] The main Seen struct control is an unusually short, conditioned subset and is not representative of a fresh IID draw.
[Reviewer-identified] The appendix says genuine IID draws behave like the nominal unseen-structure split, weakening the paper's central ID-versus-OOD terminology.
[Reviewer-identified] No behavioral training-set fidelity result supports the abstract's specific training-set statement.
[Reviewer-identified] Per-split key/query reconstruction error, explained variance, cluster distortion, and subspace angle are not reported.
[Reviewer-identified] Same Prediction is not controlled for original-model confidence or logit margin.
[Reviewer-identified] There are no random projection, matched noise, OOD-fitted SVD, joint-distribution fit, or robust-subspace controls.
[Reviewer-identified] Programming-language shift confounds language identity with syntax, length, token frequency, difficulty, and confidence.
[Reviewer-identified] The algorithmic-subtask explanation is not isolated from category frequency, margin, accuracy, and head identity.
[Reviewer-identified] The induction-head interpretation is based on visual examples without causal validation.
[Reviewer-identified] Only keys and queries of one head are simplified; values, MLPs, residual features, and complete circuits are outside scope.
[Author-stated] The models and tasks are small and limited relative to modern language models.
[Reviewer-identified] Three seeds provide weak uncertainty, and the CodeSearchNet t-tests use only three independent pairs.
[Reviewer-identified] Tests across SVD ranks receive no reported multiplicity correction or exact effect table.
[Reviewer-identified] SCAN architecture selection uses the generalization evaluation split, introducing selection leakage.
[Reviewer-identified] SCAN confidence intervals average over dependent heads rather than independent trained models.
[Reviewer-identified] Discussion sometimes calls the uncentered SVD procedure PCA, though centering is not described.
[Reviewer-identified] Proxy behavioral failure is broader than, but not equivalent to, falsifying an interpretation subsequently tested on the original model.
failure_modes: A subspace can reconstruct ID activations well but incur much larger raw projection error when the activation covariance rotates under shift.
A low-margin OOD prediction flips under a tiny benign perturbation, creating an apparent mechanistic fidelity gap.
A rare, causally important direction has low training variance and is dropped despite low average reconstruction loss.
Clustering merges states that are behaviorally interchangeable on short sequences but distinct at unseen depths.
A proxy agrees on top-1 outputs while changing calibration, secondary logits, or future autoregressive trajectories.
Hard attention improves one shift by removing distracting mass but fails a different behavior that genuinely needs distributed attention.
A dataset-defined 'ID' set becomes an easy memorization slice whose proxy agreement does not predict typical future samples.
A programming-language comparison attributes generic length or confidence sensitivity to mechanistic language transfer.
A visually induction-like head is only correlated with repeated tokens while another component supplies the causal computation.
Simplifying one head triggers compensation through residual pathways, so local fidelity does not diagnose the complete circuit.
Architecture or prompt choices selected on an OOD split exaggerate the apparent reproducibility of a gap.
An analyst mistakes a useful visualization for an executable surrogate and overclaims the domain on which it predicts behavior.
reusable_insights: Treat every interpretation as a predictive hypothesis with an explicit domain of validity, not merely an attractive visualization.
Evaluate proxy fidelity on fresh IID draws, multiple natural shifts, targeted counterexamples, and adversarially selected inputs.
Report activation reconstruction error and behavioral error jointly on every split.
Stratify agreement by original-model logit margin and compare at matched perturbation magnitude.
Fit ID-only, OOD-only, joint, and distributionally robust subspaces to distinguish missing features from ordinary covariate shift.
Use random projections and calibrated Gaussian/noise perturbations as negative controls for a named simplification method.
Test mechanistic hypotheses through interventions on the original model after using simplified views for discovery.
Separate head discovery, feature characterization, and cross-distribution validation into held-out stages.
Use independent trained models, not multiple heads of one model, as uncertainty units.
Pre-register shift taxonomies and match difficulty, length, confidence, and frequency before explaining category differences.
Measure full logit divergence, calibration, and autoregressive rollout effects in addition to top-1 agreement.
A proxy that outperforms its source is evidence that the intervention changed the algorithm, not that it faithfully explains the original.
open_questions: How much of each reported gap remains after matching ID and OOD examples by logit margin and key/query reconstruction error?
Can distributionally robust PCA, sparse autoencoders, transcoders, or nonlinear dictionaries preserve causal fidelity better than SVD and k-means?
What minimal shift suite is sufficient to bound the domain of validity of a circuit interpretation?
Can causal-abstraction metrics distinguish a wrong executable proxy from a correct qualitative hypothesis derived with that proxy?
Do full circuits exhibit larger gaps, or can redundancy make them more stable than individual heads?
How do interpretability fidelity gaps scale with model size, pretraining diversity, context length, and instruction tuning?
Can one predict OOD behavioral fidelity from unlabeled activation covariance or subspace-angle diagnostics?
Which rare low-variance features are necessary for extrapolation, and can targeted counterexample generation discover them automatically?
How stable are discovered mechanisms under natural prompt paraphrases, label permutations, languages, and model checkpoints?
Can benchmarks evaluate discovery precision, causal faithfulness, human comprehensibility, and cross-distribution prediction in one protocol?

competitive_landscape.title: Sanity Checks for Saliency Maps
competitive_landscape.relationship: Foundational predecessor for executable stress tests of explanation methods.
competitive_landscape.difference: Adebayo et al. randomize model parameters and labels to ask whether a saliency method depends on the learned model or data at all. The reviewed paper instead holds the trained model fixed, builds simplified internal proxies, and evaluates cross-distribution behavioral fidelity; it omits analogous random-projection and matched-perturbation controls.

competitive_landscape.title: Attention is not Explanation
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct antecedent questioning whether attention patterns are faithful explanations.
competitive_landscape.difference: Jain and Wallace construct alternative attention distributions with similar outputs and compare attention with feature attribution across NLP tasks. The reviewed work changes model-generated key/query representations through a fixed simplification and asks whether agreement transfers across input distributions, a different but complementary failure of attention-based interpretation.

competitive_landscape.title: Attention is not not Explanation
competitive_landscape.relationship: Methodological counterpoint defining stronger tests for attention explanations.
competitive_landscape.difference: Wiegreffe and Pinter argue that explanation validity depends on the definition and the whole trained model, proposing uniform-attention, seed-variance, diagnostic, and end-to-end adversarial tests. That critique limits any inference from a deliberately altered proxy to the validity of a hypothesis tested on the original network and motivates controls absent from the reviewed study.

competitive_landscape.title: An Interpretability Illusion for BERT
competitive_landscape.relationship: Closest conceptual predecessor and source of the interpretability-illusion framing.
competitive_landscape.difference: Bolukbasi et al. show that neurons and linear combinations can look monosemantic on a narrow corpus yet encode more complex concepts across datasets, tracing the illusion to representation geometry and dataset coverage. The reviewed paper advances from activation examples to executable proxy interventions and systematic generalization, but its representative-IID control is weaker than the framing suggests.

competitive_landscape.title: Causal Abstraction: A Theoretical Foundation for Mechanistic Interpretability
competitive_landscape.relationship: Concurrent formal framework for grading whether a simplified high-level mechanism is faithful to a neural network.
competitive_landscape.difference: Geiger et al. define faithfulness through causal abstraction and interventions, providing a way to operationalize an interpretation rather than equating it with a compressed executable network. The reviewed paper supplies valuable distribution-shift counterexamples but does not express or test the proposed human-level mechanism as a causal abstraction.

competitive_landscape.title: Does Circuit Analysis Interpretability Scale? Evidence from Multiple Choice Capabilities in Chinchilla
competitive_landscape.relationship: Very close contemporaneous study of compressed query/key/value explanations beyond their discovery distribution.
competitive_landscape.difference: Lieberum et al. compress a correct-letter head in a 70B model without loss on ordinary multiple-choice labels, then find the 'Nth item' explanation is only partial on randomized labels. The reviewed work generalizes that warning across SVD, clustering, hard attention, Dyck, code, and SCAN, but at much smaller scale and without the predecessor's large-model evidence.

competitive_landscape.title: Transformers are uninterpretable with myopic methods: a case study with bounded Dyck grammars
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct Dyck-task predecessor showing that component-local interpretations are non-identifiable.
competitive_landscape.difference: Wen et al. theoretically characterize rich sets of Dyck solutions and show that a single layer's attention can be nearly randomized without changing the network function, challenging myopic inspection even on one distribution. The reviewed paper asks a distinct generalization question: whether one fixed simplification continues to match one trained model across shifts.

competitive_landscape.title: Adaptive Circuit Behavior and Generalization in Mechanistic Interpretability
competitive_landscape.relationship: Later direct study of whether a known circuit and its component mechanisms generalize across prompt variants.
competitive_landscape.difference: Nainani et al. intervene on the established GPT-2 Small IOI circuit and find that its components are reused with added edges and adaptive behavior across variants. This supplies a positive, circuit-level complement to the reviewed paper's mostly negative proxy-fidelity results and illustrates why whole-circuit causal tests can outperform fixed local simplifications.

competitive_landscape.title: MIB: A Mechanistic Interpretability Benchmark
competitive_landscape.relationship: Later benchmark formalizing comparative evaluation of causal pathways and causal-variable features.
competitive_landscape.difference: MIB evaluates precision and concision in recovering task-relevant causal pathways or variables across four tasks and five models, and finds supervised DAS stronger than SAE features for causal-variable localization. It provides standardized causal targets missing from the reviewed proxy-agreement setup, though cross-distribution validity is not its sole focus.

competitive_landscape.title: Geometry-Adaptive Explainer for Faithful Dictionary-Based Interpretability under Distribution Shift
competitive_landscape.relationship: Recent direct successor that formalizes and mitigates OOD fidelity loss for learned feature dictionaries.
competitive_landscape.difference: Lim et al. model shift as rotation between an ID dictionary and the OOD-active subspace, derive a bound relating that geometry to causal faithfulness loss, and adapt the dictionary with unlabeled OOD activations. This directly addresses the reviewed paper's diagnostic concern for modern sparse dictionaries and supplies the missing geometric and mitigation machinery.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims that common simplified representations can appear faithful on familiar examples yet mispredict the same trained model under systematic generalization, sometimes underestimating and sometimes overestimating its performance.
novelty_assessment.evidence: It turns SVD, clustering, and one-hot attention into executable interventions and reports fidelity across Dyck structural/depth splits, Java-to-other-language CodeSearchNet, prediction categories, and SCAN, with largely consistent gaps for training-fitted proxies.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The executable-proxy evaluation is a valuable and memorable advance over visual inspection alone, and the bidirectional hard-attention counterexample is especially useful. Novelty is narrower than the framing: cross-dataset interpretability illusions, attention non-identifiability, and low-rank explanations that fail on expanded distributions already existed, including a closely related 70B Chinchilla case. More importantly, the representative-IID appendix undercuts the main ID/OOD label, and missing reconstruction- and margin-matched controls prevent attributing every gap to lost mechanistic features. The defensible contribution is a controlled multi-task demonstration that training-fitted local proxies require distributional validation, not a general disproof of mechanistic interpretations derived with simplification tools.

reviewer_notes: Read all 25 cached pages, including the complete Dyck and CodeSearchNet methods/results, the true-IID appendix, model and sampling details, every error-analysis figure, significance calculation, head-level examples, SCAN hyperparameter selection, and Figure 20 uncertainty description. Closest antecedents, contemporaneous methods, and later circuit-generalization, benchmark, and geometry-adaptation work were checked against official NeurIPS/PMLR/ACL Anthology or current arXiv records on 2026-08-23.
